stem: A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an HbA1c of 8.6% despite glyburide and metformin at maximum doses. His eGFR is normal. Pioglitazone is added.
oneliner: 56M + type 2 diabetes + HbA1c 8.6% on maximum glyburide and metformin + normal eGFR + pioglitazone added → how does it work?
ask: Pioglitazone lowers his glucose mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells
options.C: Activating the PPAR-gamma nuclear receptor to improve insulin sensitivity

why: **Pioglitazone is a thiazolidinedione.** It **binds PPAR-gamma**, a nuclear receptor, changing gene transcription so adipose, muscle and liver become **more insulin sensitive**.

drug.name: Pioglitazone
drug.how: Activates PPAR-gamma, increasing insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake
drug.watch: Fluid retention and heart failure, weight gain, fractures, bladder cancer risk (pioglitazone)

stem: A 44-year-old woman has a BMI of 33 and dark, velvety skin in the axillae and neck folds. Her fasting glucose is 168 mg/dL and her HbA1c is 8.1%. Glimepiride has caused weight gain, and metformin is started instead.
oneliner: 44F + BMI 33 + acanthosis nigricans + HbA1c 8.1% + weight gain on glimepiride + metformin started → how does it work?
ask: Metformin lowers her glucose mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Increased insulin release from beta cells
options.B: Slower carbohydrate absorption in the gut

whyNot.A: **Sulfonylureas** and meglitinides: cause weight gain and hypoglycemia

why: **Obesity + acanthosis nigricans + type 2 diabetes** = insulin resistance. **Metformin** activates AMPK, **reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis** and improves insulin sensitivity without weight gain.

drug.name: Metformin
drug.how: Activates AMPK; lowers hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases insulin sensitivity
drug.watch: GI upset, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis (avoid in renal failure, contrast, severe illness); no hypoglycemia alone

stem: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an HbA1c of 7.9% on insulin glargine and metformin. His physician adds sitagliptin to increase his own insulin release in a glucose-dependent way without causing weight gain.
oneliner: 63M + type 2 diabetes + HbA1c 7.9% on glargine and metformin + sitagliptin added → how does it work?
ask: Sitagliptin lowers his glucose mainly through which of the following?

options.B: Closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells

whyNot.B: **Sulfonylureas**: insulin release regardless of glucose, so hypoglycemia
whyNot.C: **Pioglitazone**: raises insulin sensitivity, causes weight gain
whyNot.D: **Acarbose / miglitol**: no effect on insulin release

answer: DPP-4 inhibition prolongs GLP-1 and GIP (gliptin)
why: **A drug that raises endogenous, glucose-dependent insulin release without weight gain.** **Sitagliptin blocks DPP-4**, so **GLP-1 and GIP last longer**: insulin rises and glucagon falls.

drug.name: Sitagliptin
drug.how: Blocks DPP-4, so GLP-1 and GIP persist: more glucose-dependent insulin, less glucagon
drug.watch: Pancreatitis (rare), nasopharyngitis, joint pain; weight neutral, low hypoglycemia risk

stem: A 29-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found unconscious on the floor and cannot swallow. His capillary glucose is 32 mg/dL. His roommate injects the contents of an emergency kit, and within 10 minutes he is awake and his glucose is 90 mg/dL.
oneliner: 29M + type 1 diabetes + unconscious, cannot swallow + glucose 32 + emergency kit injection + awake in 10 min → how does the drug work?
ask: The injected drug raised his glucose mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Stimulating hepatic glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
options.B: Increasing glucose uptake into skeletal muscle
options.C: Releasing glucose from skeletal muscle glycogen
options.D: Blocking glucose absorption in the intestine
options.E: Slowing the breakdown of insulin in the liver

whyNot.B: This would **lower** blood glucose, like insulin
whyNot.C: Muscle lacks **glucose-6-phosphatase** and cannot release free glucose
whyNot.D: Would **not** raise glucose, and he cannot swallow anyway

why: **Severe hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes treated by injection.** **Glucagon binds its Gs receptor in the liver**, raising cAMP, which drives **glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis**.

drug.name: Glucagon
drug.how: Gs-coupled receptor in liver: cAMP up, glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
drug.watch: Nausea and vomiting; ineffective when liver glycogen is depleted (starvation, alcohol)

stem: A 35-year-old woman has fatigue, constipation and cold intolerance. Her TSH is 24 mU/L and free T4 is low. She is started on levothyroxine and told that her symptoms will take several weeks to improve.
oneliner: 35F + fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance + TSH 24, low free T4 + levothyroxine started, benefit takes weeks → how does the hormone act in cells?
ask: The slow onset of benefit is best explained by which cellular mechanism?

options.A: Binding an intracellular receptor that changes gene transcription
options.B: Activating a Gs-coupled receptor that raises cAMP
options.E: Activating a Gq-coupled receptor that raises IP3

whyNot.B: **Fast** second-messenger signaling, as with glucagon or TSH

answer: Nuclear receptor binding and altered gene transcription (thyroid hormone)
why: **Weeks to benefit** fits a genomic effect. **Thyroid hormone is lipophilic**, enters the cell, binds a **nuclear receptor**, and changes gene transcription.

drug.name: Levothyroxine
drug.how: Converted to T3, which binds the nuclear thyroid receptor and alters transcription
drug.watch: Overreplacement: tachycardia, AF, tremor, bone loss; angina in older adults

stem: A 24-year-old man passes 8 L of urine a day after a skull fracture in a bicycle accident. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. After intranasal desmopressin his urine osmolality rises to 520 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 24M + 8 L urine/day after skull fracture + Na 148 + urine osm 90 → 520 after desmopressin → how does it act?
ask: Desmopressin concentrates his urine through which of the following signaling pathways?

options.A: Gq-coupled receptor activation with increased IP3 and calcium
options.D: Gs-coupled receptor activation with increased cAMP

why: **Dilute urine that concentrates with desmopressin** = central diabetes insipidus. **Desmopressin binds V2 receptors** on collecting duct cells; **Gs raises cAMP**, aquaporin-2 channels are inserted and water is reabsorbed.

drug.name: Desmopressin (dDAVP)
drug.how: Activates V2 receptors: Gs, cAMP, aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct
drug.use: Central diabetes insipidus, nocturnal enuresis, hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease

stem: A 52-year-old premenopausal woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is started on a monthly depot injection of leuprolide. Her estradiol rises briefly in the first week and then falls to postmenopausal levels by week 4.
oneliner: 52F + premenopausal ER-positive breast cancer + monthly leuprolide + estradiol up in week 1, then postmenopausal by week 4 → how does it work?
ask: The fall in estradiol is best explained by which of the following?

options.A: Competitive blockade of estrogen receptors in breast tissue
options.B: Continuous stimulation that downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors
options.C: Inhibition of aromatase in peripheral fat
options.E: Stimulation of inhibin release from the ovary

whyNot.C: **Anastrozole / letrozole**: not effective alone before menopause
whyNot.E: Inhibin is **not** the target of this drug

answer: Pituitary GnRH receptor downregulation (continuous GnRH agonist)
why: **Initial rise then fall with a depot GnRH analog.** **Continuous leuprolide** desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors, so **LH and FSH fall** and ovarian estrogen drops. Pulsatile dosing would stimulate instead.

drug.name: Leuprolide
drug.how: Continuous dosing downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, so LH and FSH fall
drug.use: Prostate cancer, ER-positive breast cancer, endometriosis, fibroids, precocious puberty, IVF
drug.watch: Initial flare (tumor flare in prostate cancer), hot flashes, bone loss; pulsatile use stimulates fertility

stem: A 28-year-old woman has had no periods for 8 months and has had a milky discharge from both nipples. She has been unable to conceive. Pregnancy test is negative, TSH is normal, prolactin is 180 ng/mL, and MRI shows a 7-mm pituitary lesion. Bromocriptine is started.
oneliner: 28F + amenorrhea 8 mo + milky nipple discharge + infertility + prolactin 180 + 7-mm pituitary lesion + bromocriptine → how does it work?
ask: Bromocriptine lowers her prolactin mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the pituitary
options.B: Blocking estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus
options.C: Stimulating alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem
options.E: Stimulating dopamine D2 receptors on pituitary lactotrophs

whyNot.B: **Clomiphene**: induces ovulation, does not lower prolactin
whyNot.D: Would raise **LH and FSH**, not lower prolactin

why: **Amenorrhea + galactorrhea + high prolactin + pituitary microadenoma** = prolactinoma. **Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin**; bromocriptine and cabergoline are **D2 agonists** that lower prolactin and shrink the tumor.

drug.name: Bromocriptine / cabergoline
drug.how: Stimulates D2 receptors on lactotrophs: prolactin secretion falls and tumor shrinks
drug.watch: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, psychosis; cabergoline: valvulopathy at high doses

stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a near-normal fasting glucose, but glucose readings after meals reach 260 mg/dL. His physician adds a tablet to be taken with the first bite of each meal. Two weeks later he reports flatulence, bloating and loose stools. He has had no episodes of low glucose.
oneliner: 58M + type 2 diabetes + near-normal fasting glucose + glucose 260 after meals + tablet with first bite of each meal + new flatulence, bloating, loose stools + no hypoglycemia → how does the added drug lower glucose?
ask: By which mechanism does the added drug most likely lower his glucose?

options.A: Reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis through AMP kinase activation
options.B: Closing beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channels to release insulin
options.C: Activating PPAR-gamma to improve insulin sensitivity
options.D: Blocking DPP-4 to prolong the action of GLP-1
options.E: Inhibiting brush-border enzymes that digest starch and sugars

whyNot.A: Acts mainly on the liver and lowers **fasting** glucose, which is **already near normal** here
whyNot.B: Insulin secretagogues risk **low glucose** and cause no **bloating or loose stools**; he has had **no hypoglycemia**
whyNot.C: Works over weeks on insulin sensitivity; it is not taken **with the first bite of each meal** and would not cause **flatulence and loose stools**
whyNot.D: Would not explain **flatulence, bloating and loose stools**, and has no reason to be taken **with the first bite of each meal**

answer: Inhibiting brush-border enzymes that digest starch and sugars
why: A drug taken **with the first bite of each meal** that mainly lowers **after-meal glucose**, with **flatulence and loose stools**, blocks intestinal alpha-glucosidase. Carbohydrate absorption is delayed, so glucose rises less after eating, and undigested sugar is fermented by colonic bacteria. Alone it causes **no hypoglycemia**.

drug.name: Acarbose
drug.how: Inhibits brush-border alpha-glucosidases in the small intestine, delaying breakdown of starch and disaccharides so glucose absorption is slowed and after-meal peaks fall
drug.use: Type 2 diabetes with high post-meal glucose, usually added to other drugs
drug.watch: Flatulence, bloating and diarrhea from fermentation of unabsorbed carbohydrate; no hypoglycemia alone, but if it occurs with another drug, treat with glucose, not table sugar

idea.rule: Each diabetes drug class lowers glucose at a different step; the side effect points to the site of action.
also: Metformin: less hepatic gluconeogenesis; GI upset and lactic acidosis
Sulfonylureas: close beta-cell K-ATP channels; hypoglycemia and weight gain
Thiazolidinediones: PPAR-gamma activation; edema and heart failure
DPP-4 inhibitors: prolong GLP-1; pancreatitis risk, weight neutral
